newsitem.title: USA: U.S. sees disturbing China signals on Kong Kong.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sees disturbing China signals on Kong Kong.

text.p: The State Department said this week that China has sent mixed and sometimes disturbing signals on the future of Hong Kong's legislature, human rights and press freedom after Beijing takes control there on July 1.

"Over the past year, developments in Hong Kong have sent mixed signals about some aspects of the change in sovereignty" when 150 years of British rule ends in July, it said in a report delivered to Congress.

"There have been significant positive developments since March 1996," it said, particularly China's decision to keep Chief Secretary Anson Chan and other senior Hong Kong officials in place after China takes control.

But it said "China's actions regarding the future of the legislature and the laws governing human rights and civil liberties in Hong Kong have been disturbing and have caused concern in both Hong Kong and the international community."
It said China's decision to create a provisional legislature rather than keep the present one through a transition to the new rule "raises serious concerns."

It said Washington urged open and fair elections as soon as possible of a legislature for what will become China's "Hong Kong special administrative region," and that the provisional legislature's powers be limited until then.

The U.S. report criticised China for saying Hong Kong's Bill of Rights Ordinance could not override Chinese law and for not promising to continue Hong Kong's reports to the United Nations on human rights conditions there.
It said China has stated that its own 1990 Basic Law for Hong Kong will protect human rights there.
The report also said comments by Chinese officials including Foreign Minister Qian Qichen last year "reinforced the concern about restrictions on press freedoms in Hong Kong after reversion."

It said China had given its assurance that the 1990 Basic Law guarantees press freedom. But it said Qian had said in an Asian Wall Street Journal interview in October 1996 that news reports advocating the independence of Hong Kong, Taiwan or Tibet, or containing "rumors or lies" would not be permitted.

The report said Hong Kong media coverage of China continues to be extensive and frequently critical. But it said Hong Kong reporters risk being denied permits for reporting assignments in China if they violate the reporting rules.
